title: LIMIT 500000 over a non-total ordering silently and permanently drops rows
what_is_wrong: the query caps rows with no signal when the cap binds, and it orders on `occurred_at` — a wall-clock column with no uniqueness guarantee, so rows sharing the boundary instant are cut arbitrarily (R57); the next run's window starts at `at` regardless, so nothing ever re-exports the discarded rows.

title: LIMIT 500000 silently truncates a window
what_is_wrong: A window with more than 500,000 rows is cut off with no signal — no error, no flag on the schedule, `last_status` still `succeeded` — and `ORDER BY occurred_at` is not a total order, so which rows survive the cut is undefined among same-instant rows.

title: LIMIT 500000 silently truncates a window and still reports success
what_is_wrong: The query caps rows at `maxRows` with no detection of having hit the cap, so a busy window is truncated at exactly 500,000 rows and the run is recorded `succeeded` with no signal to the customer or the operator.

title: LIMIT 500000 silently truncates an export that reports success
what_is_wrong: The query caps rows at 500,000 with no check of whether the cap was reached, so an org exceeding it in one window gets a file containing the oldest 500,000 rows and a `last_status` of `succeeded`.

title: LIMIT 500000 silently truncates an over-large window and the run still reports succeeded
what_is_wrong: the query caps the row count but nothing compares the returned count to the cap, so a busy day is truncated at exactly 500,000 rows and `runSchedule` records `status = "succeeded"` with no error.

title: LIMIT 500000 truncates a busy window silently and reports success
what_is_wrong: the query caps the result set at 500,000 rows with no detection of having hit the cap, so a window that produced more rows is exported partially and recorded as `succeeded`, contradicting the documented guarantee that concatenating a schedule's objects gives "the dataset with no gaps and no duplicated rows".

title: LIMIT 500000 truncates a window silently and the remainder is never exported
what_is_wrong: the query caps at `maxRows` with no check on whether the cap was reached, so a busy org's window is cut at an arbitrary point and the run still returns `succeeded` while the schedule advances past that window forever.

title: LIMIT 500000 truncates a window silently, and ORDER BY occurred_at has no total order
what_is_wrong: A window with more than 500k rows is cut off with no error, no marker and `status = "succeeded"`, and the cut is made at a boundary in `occurred_at`, a wall-clock value that ties freely — so which of the equal-timestamp rows survive the cut is undefined (R57: a page boundary treated as completeness on a feed the consumer takes as complete).

title: LIMIT 500000 truncates the export silently, and occurred_at is not a total order
what_is_wrong: when a window contains more than `maxRows` rows the query returns exactly `maxRows` and the run is recorded `succeeded` with no signal that anything was dropped, and because `occurred_at` is a wall-clock timestamp with ties the cut falls in the middle of a group of same-instant rows, so which rows survive is undefined (R57).

title: ListByOrg is unbounded and unpaginated
what_is_wrong: The query has no `LIMIT` and the handler streams every row for the org into one JSON array.

WHERE enabled AND next_run_at <= $1` with no `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, no claim column and no compare-and-swap, and `tick` acts on the result immediately, so N workers each select and each run the same schedule — while docs/scheduled-exports.md states "a schedule is claimed by one worker, so a due run happens once even with several workers live".

title: Nothing claims a due schedule, so every worker runs every due schedule

title: Record runs on the shutdown-cancellable context, so a successful upload can be forgotten
what_is_wrong: `Record` uses the same context that `Run` cancels on shutdown, so an upload that completes just as the process is stopping fails to persist and `next_run_at` stays in the past.

title: `hour_of_day` in a DST transition is silently shifted
what_is_wrong: `time.Date` normalises a local hour that does not exist on a spring-forward day and picks the earlier of two on a fall-back day, with no record that the run moved.

title: `hour_of_day` in a DST transition is undocumented
what_is_wrong: on a spring-forward day the configured local hour may not exist and Go normalises it forward, and on a fall-back day it occurs twice with only the `next.After(local)` guard preventing a second fire; `docs/scheduled-exports.md` says nothing about either.

title: `hour_of_day` is accepted and validated for hourly schedules that ignore it
what_is_wrong: The docs state hourly schedules ignore `hour_of_day`, and `NextRun` does, but `create` accepts and stores whatever was sent, so the value is echoed back in the list response as though it were in effect.

title: `hour_of_day` is tested at `24` but not at its accepted boundary or below zero
what_is_wrong: `Validate` rejects `< 0 || > 23` but the suite exercises only `24`, leaving `0`, `23` and `-1` unclaimed, so a boundary regression to `> 24` or `>= 23` stays green (RT10 — the deny side is sampled at one point and the allow side is not sampled adjacent to the boundary).

title: `hour_of_day` on a DST spring-forward date silently shifts
what_is_wrong: `time.Date` normalizes a local time that does not exist — an `hour_of_day` of 2 in `Europe/Berlin` on the spring-forward Sunday becomes 03:00 — and picks the first of the two occurrences on the fall-back day, so the run time moves without any indication.

title: `hourly` truncates to the UTC hour, not the customer's local hour
what_is_wrong: `time.Truncate` rounds relative to the zero time in UTC, not to the value's location, so in a zone with a non-whole-hour offset (`Asia/Kolkata` +05:30, `Asia/Kathmandu` +05:45) the "hour boundary" falls at :30 or :45 local.

title: `hourly` truncation lands on the UTC hour, not the customer's local hour
what_is_wrong: `time.Truncate` rounds absolute time since the zero instant regardless of the location, so for a zone with a sub-hour offset (`Asia/Kolkata` at +05:30, `Asia/Kathmandu` at +05:45) the run lands at :30 or :45 past the local hour, while the doc says hourly schedules "run on the hour".

title: `last_error` is omitted from the response after a successful run while `last_status` is always present

what_is_wrong: On a spring-forward day the requested wall-clock hour may not exist in `loc` and `time.Date` normalises it to a different instant, while on a fall-back day it occurs twice and `time.Date` picks one — so the run either shifts by an hour or, combined with the wall-clock-anchored window, moves relative to the previous run's coverage.

file: `internal/exports/schedule.go` — `NextRun`'s `time.Date(...)` construction and `next.AddDate(0, 0, 1)` loop, read against `window`'s fixed `24 * time.Hour` / `7 * 24 * time.Hour`
title: daily and weekly slots drift by an hour across DST transitions
what_is_wrong: the slot arithmetic is wall-clock (`AddDate` preserves the hour across a transition) while the window is a fixed duration, so on each transition the two disagree by an hour; additionally a `HourOfDay` that does not exist on a spring-forward day is normalised by `time.Date` to a different instant with no signal.

title: delete answers 204 for ids that do not exist

title: deleting a nonexistent or already-deleted schedule returns 204

title: deleting a nonexistent schedule returns 204
what_is_wrong: `ExecContext` reports no error for a `DELETE` matching zero rows and the handler never inspects `RowsAffected`, so a wrong id is indistinguishable from a successful delete.

title: deleting a nonexistent schedule returns 204
what_is_wrong: `Store.Delete` discards the `sql.Result` and its `RowsAffected`, so a DELETE that matched nothing is reported to the caller as success.

title: deleting a schedule mid-run still delivers that run's object
what_is_wrong: a `DELETE` issued while a run is in flight removes the row but does not signal the worker, whose subsequent `client.Put` still writes to the bucket and whose `Record` is then a silent no-op against a missing id.

title: deleting an unknown id reports success
what_is_wrong: The `sql.Result` is discarded, so a `DELETE` for an id that does not exist returns 204 exactly as a real deletion does.
